Crane
krān
n. (a long-necked migratory bird; used of Hezekiah's chattering in sickness and of the birds that keep their seasons)
Old English cran. The Hebrew agur is a migratory bird, named in both places beside the swallow; its cry is a harsh repeated note, which is why Hezekiah reached for it.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hezekiah, given fifteen more years after being told to set his house in order, wrote down what the sickness had been like: “Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me” (Isa 38:14). It is one of the most honest descriptions of extremity in Scripture — not eloquent prayer but the broken repeated noise of a man who cannot form sentences, with his eyes failing from looking up. His conclusion is equally plain: “What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa 38:15). Jeremiah uses the same bird for a rebuke: “Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD” (Jer 8:7). Birds keep an appointment they were never taught. A covenant people, taught for centuries, missed theirs.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the crane as a migratory fowl of the genus Ardea, with a long bill, neck and legs, and a loud harsh cry; also a machine for raising weights.

expand to see more

CRANE, n. [Sax. cran.] A migratory fowl of the genus Ardea, with a long bill, neck and legs.

The crane has a loud, harsh voice, and flies in flocks at the change of seasons.

Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter. Isa. xxxviii.

2. A machine for raising great weights.

Key Scripture

Isa 38:14 — "Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me."

Isa 38:15 — "What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul."

Jer 8:7 — "Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle and the crane and the swallow observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD."

Mat 6:26 — "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?"

Modern Corruption

Prayer is judged by its fluency, though Isaiah 38 preserves a king's prayer as the chattering of a bird and God answered it.

expand to see more

Hezekiah's own record of his prayer is a rebuke to every notion that God is moved by well-turned petitions. He chattered like a crane or a swallow; he mourned as a dove; his eyes failed with looking upward; and the whole content of it comes down to five words — O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me. That is the prayer God answered with fifteen years and a sign in the shadow on the dial. Romans says the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered, because we know not what we should pray for as we ought, and Hezekiah's chapter is that verse in narrative form. A believer who cannot pray in sentences is not therefore failing to pray. The corruption to name is not eloquence itself, which is a gift, but the assumption that God hears in proportion to a man's command of language — the very thing the Lord Jesus forbade when He said men are not heard for their much speaking.

Jeremiah's use of the crane sets a different measure. The migratory birds keep their appointed times without instruction, and the prophet's complaint is that a people who had the law, the prophets, the temple and the covenant did not know the judgment of the LORD — that is, they could not read their own season. Every generation of the church has this danger. The stork does not need to be told when to fly; a congregation with Bibles in every hand may still miss what God is doing in its own time and place, because knowing the appointed times requires not information but obedience. Hezekiah, having been spared, said he would go softly all his years, and that phrase is the right posture for anyone who has been brought back from the edge and given time he did not earn.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew agur (H5693), a crane or migratory bird; with sus (H5483), the swallow, and moed (H4150), an appointed time or season.

expand to see more

Hebrew agur (H5693) — a crane; like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter; Isaiah 38:14, Jeremiah 8:7.

Hebrew tsaphaph (H6850) — to chirp or peep; the sound Hezekiah made in his sickness; Isaiah 38:14.

Hebrew moed (H4150) — an appointed time; the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times; Jeremiah 8:7.

Hebrew chasidah (H2624) — the stork, literally the kind or faithful one; Jeremiah 8:7.

Hebrew arab (H6148) — to be surety, to undertake for; undertake for me; Isaiah 38:14.

Usage

"“Like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter” — a king's prayer, described by its owner."

"“O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me” — five words, and fifteen years granted."

"“My people know not the judgment of the LORD” — birds keep an appointment men missed."
